system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by post-bypass hypoglycemia requiring a gastrostomy tube and status post bypass reversal was readmitted five days after a prior discharge with recurrent constant abdominal pain localized to the G-tube site radiating to the left flank and repeated emesis with oral intake. She was managed conservatively with NPO and IV fluids, venting of the G-tube (which appeared patent), and symptom control with antiemetics and non-NSAID analgesia while continuing gastric mucosal protection (pantoprazole and sucralfate) and resuming home medications as tolerated. Plain films showed no free air or obstruction, and CT abdomen/pelvis with IV and oral contrast demonstrated normal-appearing anastomoses and appropriately positioned G-tube without obstruction, abscess, or other acute process. Diet was advanced and tolerated, nutrition assessment indicated oral intake >75% of requirements, and blood glucose remained within normal limits throughout hospitalization; she was discharged home ambulatory with oral ondansetron, continued PPI/sucralfate and dronabinol for appetite, limited liquid opioid for breakthrough pain, and instructions for outpatient hypoglycemia dietary management and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with a lot of diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, and worsening belly pain around the G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on since you left the hospital last week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was bad pain near the tube, but the oxycodone kept it under control. Then two days ago I started having nonstop diarrhea—like more than nine times a day—and I couldn’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Any fevers or chills? Anyone around you sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No sick contacts that I know of.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting—when did that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday. My surgeon told me to try Imodium, and after I took it I got really nauseated and threw up like eight times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The last time had little specks of blood. I was retching a lot. No black stools though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that detail helps. Small streaks after repeated retching can be from irritation in the throat or upper stomach, but we’ll keep a close eye on it. Right now your blood pressure and oxygen look okay, and your labs in the ER didn’t show infection or kidney trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s something wrong with the tube or my surgery again. The pain is right there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. Bariatric Surgery has already weighed in and doesn’t think this looks like a surgical complication today. Your belly exam is tender but soft, and there’s no guarding. We’ll still be cautious and check for things like obstruction if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what are you doing for me now? I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, IV fluids to treat dehydration from the diarrhea and vomiting. Second, nausea medicine through the IV. Third, pain control—starting with IV medication while you can’t tolerate pills, then switching back to your liquid oxycodone when you’re able to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—please don’t give those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin. We’ll use options that are safe with your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also going to send stool tests. Given the volume of diarrhea, we want to rule out C. difficile and check for viral causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. Could it be back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, so we’re testing. The good news is your white blood cell count is normal and you don’t have a fever, which makes severe bacterial infection less likely, but the stool test will help us be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is so dry. Am I really that dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your exam shows dry mucous membranes, and with more than nine diarrheal stools a day it adds up quickly. The IV fluids should help you feel better over the next several hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any more vomiting since you arrived?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting here. Still diarrhea though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now and slowly reintroduce liquids when your nausea is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your abdominal pain and G-tube history, we’re getting a plain abdominal X-ray to look at the bowel gas pattern and make sure there’s no obstruction or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a CT scan? I don’t want a lot of radiation again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s much less radiation than a CT. It’s a quick X-ray—helpful as a screening test when the exam is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain meds help, but I’m scared I’ll be stuck on them. I only feel okay when it’s scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to treat the acute pain while your stomach and intestines recover, then step back to the lowest amount you need. Today we’ll use IV medication only while you can’t take anything by mouth, and we’ll switch back to your home liquid oxycodone as soon as you’re tolerating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows no obstruction or ileus and no free air. The G-tube is seen in the left upper abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no evidence of blockage on the X-ray, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my stomach meds? I’m worried about my ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re continuing acid protection. While you’re not eating much, we’ll start with IV proton pump inhibitor, then switch back to your home pantoprazole by mouth when you can tolerate it, along with ranitidine and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We collected the stool sample tonight. Results will take some time, but we should have the C. diff test back soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting or more blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No more blood. Still crampy and going to the bathroom a lot, but maybe a little less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your electrolytes and kidney function look stable this morning. We’ll keep IV fluids going and recheck labs as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile test is negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stool viral panel came back positive for norovirus. That’s a common, very contagious viral gastroenteritis that causes sudden diarrhea and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—antibiotics don’t help norovirus. Treatment is supportive: fluids, nausea control, and time. Most people improve over a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did the Imodium make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can in some cases—slowing the gut during an infection can make people feel more bloated or nauseated. The key now is hydration and letting your body clear the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you haven’t vomited here, we can try sips of clear liquids and then advance to a light bariatric diet as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to eat. Every time I try at home, I get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. We’ll go slowly—small amounts, frequent sips, and we’ll give ondansetron as needed. If nausea returns, we pause and step back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube—should I vent it like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel very bloated or nauseated, venting can sometimes help, but right now your symptoms fit norovirus more than a tube problem. We’ll have nursing help you if you need to vent it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now that you’ve had some fluids and nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still sore around the G-tube, but not as sharp. I’d like to switch off the IV meds if I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. If you’re tolerating liquids, we can transition from IV morphine to your oral liquid oxycodone every 4 hours as needed, like your prior discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take dronabinol for appetite, but I think I reacted to it before. Are you giving it to me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding dronabinol during this gastroenteritis, especially since you reported a possible prior reaction. Once you’re fully recovered, you can discuss whether to restart it with your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You had a low-grade temperature overnight but you look much better. How many diarrheal episodes since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Way fewer. I’m still going, but it’s not constant. I kept down the bariatric tray last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s what we need to see: improving diarrhea and reliable oral intake. Your labs this morning look stable as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the blood specks I had at home—do I need a scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it was small volume, happened after repeated vomiting, and you’ve had no further vomiting or bleeding here, it’s most consistent with irritation from retching. We’re continuing your acid-suppressing meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate. If you have recurrent vomiting with blood, black stools, or feel faint, you should seek care right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I contagious? I don’t want my husband to get this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Norovirus is very contagious. At home, wash hands with soap and water, clean high-touch surfaces, and avoid preparing food for others until you’re fully better. If possible, use a separate bathroom for a couple of days after symptoms stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge today if you continue to tolerate food and your symptoms keep improving. Any concerns about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the pain will spike again and I’ll end up back here. And I still want this G-tube out eventually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain, we’ll send you home on the same liquid oxycodone plan you had before, plus acetaminophen as needed—no NSAIDs. For the G-tube, that decision should be made with your bariatric surgery team once your oral intake is consistently good; we’ll make sure you have follow-up arranged with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw something about protein in my urine. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urinalysis showed a small amount of protein. It can happen transiently with illness or dehydration. We recommend repeating it with your outpatient doctor once you’re recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep all my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your home medications: fluoxetine and aripiprazole for mood, lorazepam as needed for anxiety, gabapentin for neuropathy, atorvastatin for cholesterol, and zolpidem as needed for sleep. Continue pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate for stomach protection, and ondansetron as needed for nausea. We’re recommending you do not restart dronabinol until you’ve fully recovered and have discussed it with your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more item: we sent a rectal swab to screen for resistant bacteria while you were here. It came back with no VRE isolated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And diet—what am I supposed to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on Bariatric Diet Stage 5. Keep portions small, focus on what you tolerate, and prioritize hydration. If diarrhea worsens again and you can’t keep fluids down, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also want to switch to a new primary care doctor. Can you help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’ll give you the information to establish with a new PCP and instructions on how to transfer your records. It’s important for follow-up on the urine protein, your nutrition, and medication management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: your diagnosis is norovirus gastroenteritis. You improved with IV fluids, nausea control, and pain management, and you’re now eating and drinking. Do you feel ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still tired, but I’m not vomiting and the diarrhea is better. I just want to recover at home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by post-bypass hypoglycemia requiring a gastrostomy tube and status post bypass reversal was admitted with acute onset of large-volume diarrhea (>9/day), nausea/vomiting with small blood specks after retching, and worsened abdominal pain near the G-tube with poor oral intake. Evaluation showed stable labs and reassuring abdominal exam; abdominal X-ray demonstrated no obstruction or free air. Stool testing was negative for toxigenic C. difficile and positive for norovirus, and she was managed supportively with IV fluids, serial electrolyte monitoring, antiemetics, gastric mucosal protection (IV then oral PPI with ranitidine and sucralfate), and analgesia transitioned from IV morphine to home liquid oxycodone as oral intake improved. Symptoms steadily improved with tolerance of a light bariatric diet (Stage 5) and decreased diarrhea; she was discharged home ambulatory with continuation of home medications, ondansetron as needed, dronabinol held pending outpatient follow-up, and plans for outpatient reassessment of mild proteinuria and bariatric surgery follow-up regarding potential future G-tube removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with a lot of diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, and worsening belly pain around the G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on since you left the hospital last week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was bad pain near the tube, but the oxycodone kept it under control. Then two days ago I started having nonstop diarrhea—like more than nine times a day—and I couldn’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds miserable. Any fevers or chills? Anyone around you sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers. No sick contacts that I know of.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the vomiting—when did that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yesterday. My surgeon told me to try Imodium, and after I took it I got really nauseated and threw up like eight times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The last time had little specks of blood. I was retching a lot. No black stools though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that detail helps. Small streaks after repeated retching can be from irritation in the throat or upper stomach, but we’ll keep a close eye on it. Right now your blood pressure and oxygen look okay, and your labs in the ER didn’t show infection or kidney trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s something wrong with the tube or my surgery again. The pain is right there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. Bariatric Surgery has already weighed in and doesn’t think this looks like a surgical complication today. Your belly exam is tender but soft, and there’s no guarding. We’ll still be cautious and check for things like obstruction if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what are you doing for me now? I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, IV fluids to treat dehydration from the diarrhea and vomiting. Second, nausea medicine through the IV. Third, pain control—starting with IV medication while you can’t tolerate pills, then switching back to your liquid oxycodone when you’re able to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to NSAIDs and aspirin—please don’t give those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—no NSAIDs or aspirin. We’ll use options that are safe with your allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also going to send stool tests. Given the volume of diarrhea, we want to rule out C. difficile and check for viral causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. Could it be back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, so we’re testing. The good news is your white blood cell count is normal and you don’t have a fever, which makes severe bacterial infection less likely, but the stool test will help us be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is so dry. Am I really that dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your exam shows dry mucous membranes, and with more than nine diarrheal stools a day it adds up quickly. The IV fluids should help you feel better over the next several hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: any more vomiting since you arrived?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting here. Still diarrhea though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now and slowly reintroduce liquids when your nausea is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your abdominal pain and G-tube history, we’re getting a plain abdominal X-ray to look at the bowel gas pattern and make sure there’s no obstruction or free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that like a CT scan? I don’t want a lot of radiation again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s much less radiation than a CT. It’s a quick X-ray—helpful as a screening test when the exam is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain meds help, but I’m scared I’ll be stuck on them. I only feel okay when it’s scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to treat the acute pain while your stomach and intestines recover, then step back to the lowest amount you need. Today we’ll use IV medication only while you can’t take anything by mouth, and we’ll switch back to your home liquid oxycodone as soon as you’re tolerating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows no obstruction or ileus and no free air. The G-tube is seen in the left upper abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing is blocked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no evidence of blockage on the X-ray, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I take my stomach meds? I’m worried about my ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re continuing acid protection. While you’re not eating much, we’ll start with IV proton pump inhibitor, then switch back to your home pantoprazole by mouth when you can tolerate it, along with ranitidine and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We collected the stool sample tonight. Results will take some time, but we should have the C. diff test back soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting or more blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. No more blood. Still crampy and going to the bathroom a lot, but maybe a little less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your electrolytes and kidney function look stable this morning. We’ll keep IV fluids going and recheck labs as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. difficile test is negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stool viral panel came back positive for norovirus. That’s a common, very contagious viral gastroenteritis that causes sudden diarrhea and vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No—antibiotics don’t help norovirus. Treatment is supportive: fluids, nausea control, and time. Most people improve over a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did the Imodium make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can in some cases—slowing the gut during an infection can make people feel more bloated or nauseated. The key now is hydration and letting your body clear the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you haven’t vomited here, we can try sips of clear liquids and then advance to a light bariatric diet as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared to eat. Every time I try at home, I get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear makes sense. We’ll go slowly—small amounts, frequent sips, and we’ll give ondansetron as needed. If nausea returns, we pause and step back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My tube—should I vent it like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel very bloated or nauseated, venting can sometimes help, but right now your symptoms fit norovirus more than a tube problem. We’ll have nursing help you if you need to vent it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now that you’ve had some fluids and nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still sore around the G-tube, but not as sharp. I’d like to switch off the IV meds if I can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. If you’re tolerating liquids, we can transition from IV morphine to your oral liquid oxycodone every 4 hours as needed, like your prior discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I used to take dronabinol for appetite, but I think I reacted to it before. Are you giving it to me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding dronabinol during this gastroenteritis, especially since you reported a possible prior reaction. Once you’re fully recovered, you can discuss whether to restart it with your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You had a low-grade temperature overnight but you look much better. How many diarrheal episodes since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Way fewer. I’m still going, but it’s not constant. I kept down the bariatric tray last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That’s what we need to see: improving diarrhea and reliable oral intake. Your labs this morning look stable as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the blood specks I had at home—do I need a scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because it was small volume, happened after repeated vomiting, and you’ve had no further vomiting or bleeding here, it’s most consistent with irritation from retching. We’re continuing your acid-suppressing meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate. If you have recurrent vomiting with blood, black stools, or feel faint, you should seek care right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I contagious? I don’t want my husband to get this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Norovirus is very contagious. At home, wash hands with soap and water, clean high-touch surfaces, and avoid preparing food for others until you’re fully better. If possible, use a separate bathroom for a couple of days after symptoms stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning discharge today if you continue to tolerate food and your symptoms keep improving. Any concerns about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried the pain will spike again and I’ll end up back here. And I still want this G-tube out eventually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For pain, we’ll send you home on the same liquid oxycodone plan you had before, plus acetaminophen as needed—no NSAIDs. For the G-tube, that decision should be made with your bariatric surgery team once your oral intake is consistently good; we’ll make sure you have follow-up arranged with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw something about protein in my urine. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urinalysis showed a small amount of protein. It can happen transiently with illness or dehydration. We recommend repeating it with your outpatient doctor once you’re recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep all my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue your home medications: fluoxetine and aripiprazole for mood, lorazepam as needed for anxiety, gabapentin for neuropathy, atorvastatin for cholesterol, and zolpidem as needed for sleep. Continue pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate for stomach protection, and ondansetron as needed for nausea. We’re recommending you do not restart dronabinol until you’ve fully recovered and have discussed it with your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more item: we sent a rectal swab to screen for resistant bacteria while you were here. It came back with no VRE isolated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And diet—what am I supposed to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on Bariatric Diet Stage 5. Keep portions small, focus on what you tolerate, and prioritize hydration. If diarrhea worsens again and you can’t keep fluids down, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also want to switch to a new primary care doctor. Can you help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—we’ll give you the information to establish with a new PCP and instructions on how to transfer your records. It’s important for follow-up on the urine protein, your nutrition, and medication management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: your diagnosis is norovirus gastroenteritis. You improved with IV fluids, nausea control, and pain management, and you’re now eating and drinking. Do you feel ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still tired, but I’m not vomiting and the diarrhea is better. I just want to recover at home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by post-bypass hypoglycemia requiring a gastrostomy tube and status post bypass reversal was admitted with acute onset of large-volume diarrhea (>9/day), nausea/vomiting with small blood specks after retching, and worsened abdominal pain near the G-tube with poor oral intake. Evaluation showed stable labs and reassuring abdominal exam; abdominal X-ray demonstrated no obstruction or free air. Stool testing was negative for toxigenic C. difficile and positive for norovirus, and she was managed supportively with IV fluids, serial electrolyte monitoring, antiemetics, gastric mucosal protection (IV then oral PPI with ranitidine and sucralfate), and analgesia transitioned from IV morphine to home liquid oxycodone as oral intake improved. Symptoms steadily improved with tolerance of a light bariatric diet (Stage 5) and decreased diarrhea; she was discharged home ambulatory with continuation of home medications, ondansetron as needed, dronabinol held pending outpatient follow-up, and plans for outpatient reassessment of mild proteinuria and bariatric surgery follow-up regarding potential future G-tube removal.
